COURT

th
, 2015

OF:
THE
HONOURABLE KAREN KEAR JODOIN, J.S.C.

_____________________________________________________________________________

D. S.

Plaintiff

Vs.-

J. S.

Defendant

judgment on custody and access  rights

[
1
]

The
Court must make a very difficult decision as to which of these two loving,
devoted and competent parents should be awarded custody of X born on the […]
2006, presently nine years of age.

[
2
]

The Father believes that it is in X’s best
interest that he remains in his custody in the city A. He states that X has
been under his care during the last three years and that the child is well
integrated in this city. Father states that he is best able to provide X with
the stability and security that he requires.

[
3
]

Mother states that in 2008, the parties agreed
that they would share custody of X on a year-to-year alternating basis. She adds that the parties subsequently verbally agreed that X’s
residence would alternate every two years. However, as a result of certain
circumstances, the child remained with Father for three years. She believes
that it is in X’s best interest to reside with her in Washington, D.C. At
trial, she undertook to return the child to the Father in city A in three years
when X commences secondary school. The Court notes that the plan of
argumentation submitted by Mother indicates the “possibility” of the child
returning to city A to begin his secondary school in 2018.

CONTEXT

[
4
]

The parties were married on September 1, 2001,
in San Francisco, California.

[
5
]

Prior to marriage, both parties were employed as
lawyers. The Father was employed in Vancouver and upon marriage; he left his
employment to relocate to San Francisco.

[
6
]

When X was born on [...], 2006, the parties were
residing in San Francisco. Father was employed as a [...] of San Francisco.
Mother was completing a book for publication.

[
7
]

In 2007, Mother accepted a position to become a
Foreign Service Officer for the United States. In March 2007, Mother relocated
to Washington, for a six month training program. After Mother’s departure, Father
remained in San Francisco for approximately two months and cared for X with the
help of the maternal grandmother.

[
8
]

In May 2007, Father and X joined Mother in
Washington.

[
9
]

In 2007, Mother obtained a two-year posting to
Jerusalem, Israel. The family moved in Jerusalem. Father was able to secure
part-time employment as an investigator for the U.S. State Department.

[
10
]

In October 2008, the parties experienced
matrimonial difficulties. Father and X returned to Canada and resided with
Father’s parents in North Bay, Ontario until April 2009.

[
11
]

In March 2009, Father secured employment with
the [Company A] and was required to complete six months of training in Regina,
Alberta. X returned to Jerusalem and remained in Mother’s care from March 2009
until December 2009.

[
12
]

From January 2010 until September 2010, X’s
residences alternated between Mother and Father in North Bay, city A,
Washington or Fresno.

[
13
]

From September 2010 until June 2010, both Mother
and Father were posted in the city A. They lived separate and apart and shared
custody of X on a week to week basis. Both parties were employed on a full time
basis and X attended daycare.

[
14
]

In 2011, X commenced kindergarten in the city A.

[
15
]

In June 2012, Mother left her posting in city A
and shared custody of X on a week to week basis was no longer viable.

[
16
]

On June 18, 2012, in anticipation of Mother’s
departure from city A, the parties attended mediation and reached an agreement
setting the consequences of the breakdown of their marriage, including custody
of X. The agreement provides among others, as follows
[1]
:

(…)

ix.

During the 2014-2015 school year, X’s residence
will be with his mother, wherever she resides.

x.

During 2015-2016 school year, X’s residence will
be with his father in city A.

xi.

During 2016-2017 school year, X’s residence is
expected to be with his mother providing that the timing of her relocation does
not interfere with the school year. In the event that Ms. S.’s residence is not
stable for the entire school year, X’s residence will continue to be in city A
with his father, in order to maintain consistency and stability during the
school year.

xii.

During the 2017-2018 school year, X’s residence
is expected to be with his father in city A.

(…)

[
17
]

On December 12, 2012, Mother gave birth to Y, a
child born of her current relationship with her common law spouse.

[
18
]

Mother was deployed to Pakistan from April 2013
until April 2014.

[
19
]

On February 26, 2013, a judgment of divorce was
granted by the Fresno County Superior Court. The judgment did not ratify the
mediated agreement, but included the following provision relating to custody of
X
[2]
:

The parties shall have joint
legal and physical custody of the minor child, X, born [...], 2006. X shall
reside with each parent on an alternating one week basis with the exchange
occurring on Sunday mornings unless otherwise agreed in writing. X shall have
custodial time with the non-custodial parent so as to ensure that he does not
go a full week without seeing the other parent. The parents shall share X’s
birthday equally. Holidays and special occasion times shall be shared between
the parents.

[
20
]

On April 14, 2014, Father filed a motion for custody of X in the
Fresno County Superior Court
[3]
. Mother received the proceedings while she was still in Pakistan.
She also notes that Father retained new counsel in California in January 2014
[4]
. She asserts that Father's application for custody was calculated
and premeditated.

[
21
]

On August 8, 2014 temporary ruling was rendered
by the Fresno Superior Court, which provided that X would remain with his Father
during school time and non‑school time would be with Mother, the whole
until the merits of the matter were heard. A date for hearing was scheduled for
the 10
th
, 11
th
and 12
th
day of December 2014.

[
22
]

On December 2, 2014, the Fresno Superior Court
declined jurisdiction
[5]
.

[
23
]

On December 2, 2014, Mother is served with Father
application to the Superior Court of Québec for custody of X.

[
24
]

On December 11, 2014, Mother applied to the
Superior Court of Québec, requesting the homologation of the mediated agreement
dated June 18, 2012, and that X reside with her for a term of three years
commencing September 2015. She further requested that the Court confirm joint
custody of X. At trial Mother amended her motion requesting in the alternative
custody of X in the event that joint custody is not viable.

WHAT CUSTODY ARRANGEMENT IS IN THE BEST INTEREST OF X ?

[
25
]

The Court is guided by the principles set out at
section 17.(5) of the
Divorce Act
,  which provides as follows:

17.(5)   Before the court makes a
variation order in respect of a custody order, the court shall satisfy itself
that there has been a change in the condition, means, needs or other
circumstances of the child of the marriage occurring since the making of the
custody order or the last variation order made in respect of that order, as the
case may be, and, in making the variation order, the court shall take into
consideration only the best interests of the child as determined by reference
to that change.
[6]

[
26
]

The parties agree that there has been a change
of circumstances since the rendering of the divorce judgment. The judgment of
divorce provides that custody of X shall alternate on a week to week basis.
This arrangement has not been viable since Mother's departure from city A in
2012. No explanation was given to the Court as to why the mediated agreement
[7]
was not ratified by the Fresno Superior Court.

[
27
]

Mother asserts that the parties had verbally
agreed to amend the mediated agreement to provide that custody of X would
alternate on a two-year basis. In any event both parties agree that the judgment
of divorce on the mediated agreement, which calls for the custody of X to
alternate on a year-to-year basis, is not in the best interest of the child. The
Court agrees the result of such an arrangement would be that every year, X
would be uprooted and his life disrupted in a major way. The Court is of the
view that in the absence of compelling factors, alternating a child's residence
and school, in order to give each parent equal time with the child is not in the
child's best interest. Clearly, such an arrangement sacrifices the child for
the benefit of the parents.

[
28
]

In view of the foregoing the Court is satisfied
that there has been a material change to warrant a variation order. What
arrangement best serves the interests of young X?

[
29
]

The circumstances in this case are exceptionally
difficult. However, it is evident that the consideration that must guide the
Court's decision of this kind of case is the best interest of the child.

[
30
]

Although, the matter before the Court is not a
question of relocation per se as contemplated by
Gordon
vs.
Goert
z
[8]
, the legal principles set out therein, adapted as necessary, are
also up applicable to the case at bar. Justice McLachlin (as she was then) states
as follows
[9]
:

[49]  The law can be summarized as follows:

i.

The parent applying for a change in the custody
or access order must meet the threshold requirement of demonstrating a material
change in the circumstances affecting the child.

ii.

If the threshold is met, the judge on the
application must embark on a fresh inquiry into what is in the best interests
of the child, having regard to all the relevant circumstances relating to the
child’s needs and the ability of the respective parents to satisfy them.

iii.

This inquiry is based on the findings of the
judge who made the previous order and evidence of the new circumstances.

iv.

The inquiry does not begin with a legal
presumption in favour of the custodial parent, although the custodial parent’s
views are entitled to great respect.

v.

Each case turns on its own unique circumstances.
The only issue is the best interest of the child in the particular
circumstances of the case.

vi.

The focus is on the best interests of the child,
not the interests and rights of the parents.

vii.

More particularly the judge should consider,
inter
alia
:

1.

the existing custody arrangement and the
relationship between the child and the custodial parent;

2.

the existing access arrangement and the
relationship between the child and the access parent;

3.

the desirability of maximizing contact between
the child and both parents;

4.

the views of the child;

5.

the custodial parent’s reason for moving, only
in the exceptional case where it is relevant to that parent’s ability to meet
the needs of the child;

6.

disruption to the child of a change in custody;

7.

disruption to the child consequent on removal
from family, schools, and the community he or she has come to know.

[50]   In the end, the
importance of the child remaining with the parent to whose custody it has
become accustomed in the new location must be weighed against the continuance
of full contact with the child’s access parent, its extended family and its
community.
The ultimate question in every case is this: what is in the best
interests of the child in all the circumstances, old as well as new
?

(Emphasis my own)

[
31
]

The undisputed evidence is that both parents are
exemplary. Each parent describes the other in glowing terms. X has the good
fortune to have two loving and competent parents. He is also blessed to share a
close and loving bond with both his maternal and paternal grandparents, all of
whom are actively involved in his life.

[
32
]

Mother maintains that the residence of X should
rotate on a three-year basis. Such an arrangement would enable X to have the
opportunity to strengthen his bond with his younger brother Y. She suggests
that X returns to city A once he commences secondary school. She offers to pay
the cost of private schooling at a C school in Washington, to ensure a smooth
transition from elementary school in Washington to a secondary school in city A.
She also offers to pay for French private schooling for secondary school in the
city A.

[
33
]

However, to ensure that X maintains a close
relationship with his Father, she offers almost all nonschool days to Father
and is prepared to pay half of the travel costs for X to visit with him.
Moreover, she is prepared to assume a portion of Father's travel cost to visit
Washington, and reasonable costs of his accommodations.

[
34
]

Mother is angered by Father’s failure to respect
their mediated agreement. She states that parties were well aware of certain
disruptions to X’s life but agreed in 2012 that the child would have maximum
contact with both parents. She asserts that Father has orchestrated a false
status
quo
in order to demonstrate that X is well integrated in the city A. The
evidence reveals that X attends Torah School and attends religious services at
Temple Beth L. Emmanuel. Although Mother acknowledges that she wants X to be
raised in the Jewish faith, she maintains that it has not been the family
practice to attend synagogue each and every weekend. She believes that Father
has established “artificial roots” in the community.

[
35
]

She also has concerns with regard to Father's
choice of schools. She does not believe that the child is thriving as asserted
by Father. She believes, contrary to Father's assertion, that X is not a gifted
musician. She states that the child's report cards indicate that his
performance at school is far from stellar.

[
36
]

X is described by all witnesses as intelligent,
creative, curious, happy and a well-balanced child. He sings and plays piano.
He also plays violin with limited success.

[
37
]

Mother contends that X is a resilient child and
will easily adapt to the transition to Washington. All witnesses confirm that X
is well able to adapt to new situations. He is attended day camps in both North
Bay and Fresno and all grandparents acknowledge that he is a very social child
and that he makes friends easily.

[
38
]

Father acknowledges that Mother is an excellent
parent. However, he believes that she has placed her career aspirations before
her parenting responsibilities. He states that he has always accommodated Mother's
work schedule. He notes Mother's posting in Jerusalem and underscores that when
Mother accepted a one-year post in Pakistan, she left her five-month-old child
to be cared for by her parents in Fresno and X in his care.

[
39
]

Father states that Mother missed X's first day
at school. When she was offered to care for the child while Father was on a
hunting trip, Mother declined, preferring to return to Europe to be with her
boyfriend.

[
40
]

Father expresses concerns that Mother's new
relationship is not stable.

[
41
]

More importantly, he states that the essence of
Mother's career is that she must travel. Although, Mother acknowledges that her
work requires her to travel, she undertakes to remain in Washington, for a
minimum of three years.

[
42
]

The parties have different views as to who was
the primary parent to X. Father asserts that he has always been the primary
parent and that he has always placed his interests secondary to those of X.
Mother maintains that she has been the primary parent to X.

[
43
]

The Court does not make any finding with respect
to the parties' submissions as to who was the primary parent. The evidence
amply reveals that both parties have made a significant contribution to the
upbringing of their son. Clearly, this decision cannot be based on a finding that
one parent is more fit than the other. Both parents are beyond reproach and
have much to offer young X.

[
44
]

Father states that his hours of employment are
stable and he has greater availability then Mother. He asserts that mother
works long hours. Mother asserts her hours are flexible and Father does not
have sufficient time for extracurricular activities other than music and Torah
school. The Court finds that the availability of each parent is similar and
therefore it is not an issue to be considered.

[
45
]

Let us consider X's life with Father.

[
46
]

X and his Father live in a condominium in
downtown city A. Father is employed with the [Company A] as a Specialized […]. Father's
hours of employment are from 8:00 AM until 4:00 PM.

[
47
]

Father describes a typical day with X as
follows: they have breakfast and then X is dropped off at daycare at 7:30 AM.
At 8:25 AM X travels by bus to l’École A. School starts at 9:00 AM and ends at
4:10 PM. Father is able to meet with X at 4:45. Homework is completed and
thereafter dinner is served. X enjoys “face time” with his Mother every evening
for approximately 30 minutes.

[
48
]

During weekends, they do various activities
including hiking and biking.

[
49
]

École A is a multicultural school that offers a
curriculum which emphasizes music instruction. The academic curriculum is
completed within 60% of school time; the balance of time is devoted to music.

[
50
]

Father maintains that X is musically gifted. He
states that he enrolled X at Ecole A , upon the recommendation of X's former
school. The paternal grandparents praised Father's choice of schools and the Mother
did not object to same.

[
51
]

X's report cards do not indicate that he is a
gifted musician. However, his grades are well within average, especially when
one considers that he is an Anglophone attending a French educational institution.
Father is fluently bilingual and is able to help X with his studies.

[
52
]

X has a network of friends both at school, at
Temple and in the neighbourhood.

[
53
]

Every Saturday at X attends Temple Beth El
Emanuel. He attends Torah School. He attends family services with his Father.
Father states that he is fulfilling his commitment to Mother that X would be raised
in the Jewish faith. Both Father and X have developed friendships at the
synagogue.

[
54
]

Mother can also offer an enriching albeit
different environment for X.

[
55
]

Mother resides in […]. She describes the area as
the "Westmount" of Washington.

[
56
]

Mother initially enrolled X at B School, which
is walking distance from her residence. Shortly prior to trial, she enrolled
the child at a C School, which would allow X to pursue his French studies
[10]
. A representative of the school testified and indicated that the
curriculum followed is similar to that of D School in city A. The cost of
tuition is $16,000. US per year. It is located approximately 45 minutes from Mother's
residence. X would leave for school at approximately 8:15 AM and return home by
4:45 PM.

[
57
]

One challenge that some children face at this
school is with respect to the completion of their homework when their parents
have limited knowledge of the French language.

[
58
]

Mother asserts that her hours are flexible and
that she does not anticipate any postings outside Washington in the foreseeable
future
[11]
.

[
59
]

Mother undertakes to ensure that X continues
both his piano lessons and his Hebrew lessons. She states that the
extracurricular and cultural activities for X in Washington are limitless. She
is confident that X shall have no difficulties making friends in the
neighbourhood or at his new school.

[
60
]

Most importantly, Mother wants X to spend the
next three years growing with his younger sibling Y. The evidence reveals that X
has developed a very close and loving relationship with his younger brother.
The video presented at the Court speaks volumes
[12]
. She
also states that X's shares a very good relationship with her common law partner
B....

[
61
]

The Court finds that X should remain in Father's
custody until the child finishes primary school at which time custody shall be
subject to review.

[
62
]

The major consideration in this case is the
present living arrangements of the respective parties and the child's history
since the date of separation. The Court cannot predict the future with
certainty, so it must make the best judgment as it can as to which course for
the child's is in his best interest and appears to hold fewer risks.

[
63
]

The evidence reveals that X has resided mostly
with Father. During the years from 2007 until 2010, Father adjusted his
employment and career plans to accommodate Mother's work schedule and to care
for X. He left his employment in San Francisco as a [...] to relocate to
Jerusalem for two years. Mother was employed on a full-time basis and Father
assumed the lion share of childcare responsibilities.

[
64
]

When the parties separated in 2008 Father and X
left Jerusalem and returned to Canada. Mother remained in Jerusalem until the
end of her posting.

[
65
]

There is no doubt having regard to Mother's
resources that she can offer a higher standard of living for X than Father. She
describes herself as independently wealthy. However, this is not a factor that
the Court should consider in determining what custody arrangement is in the
child's best interest. The lifestyles offered by the parties may differ but
both are more than suitable and appropriate.

[
66
]

The Court finds that the three-year rotation of
residence of X as suggested by Mother is too disruptive. At present, X has an
established network of friends in the neighbourhood, at school and at
synagogue. They are not “artificial roots”. He has resided in the city A since
2010. It is not in his best interest to uproot him at the present time. This
would require X to adapt to a new home, a new neighbourhood and the third
change of schools in three years. Moreover, X would be required to adapt to a new
family dynamic sharing his Mother not only with his younger sibling Y, but with
her common law partner B....

[
67
]

The Court appreciates Mother's desire that X
and Y grow up together. As a general rule our Court is loathe to separate
siblings. However, this is the reality experienced by Y and X. They have never
lived under the same roof save and except during holidays and summer months.
Despite the fact that they have not lived together, the children have managed
to develop a close and loving relationship that can be nurtured maintained for
the time being with extended access. The Court also notes that there is a
significant difference in age of the two siblings; Y is two years old and X is
nine years old.

[
68
]

Mother has offered numerous safeguards to ensure
that X returns to city A in three years. Although the Court does not doubt Mother's
good faith, there is no guarantee that the child will return to city A in three
years.

[
69
]

The evidence before the Court reveals that X
must change schools after he completes Grade 6. Custody shall be reviewed at
that time. The Court reminds Father that he has on numerous occasions
acknowledged that it was in the best interest of X to have maximum contact with
both parents. Although, the Court does not have a crystal ball, the Court would
encourage Father to consider seriously that the child’s residence be with
Mother once X has finished primary school. X should be afforded the opportunity
to experience daily life with both parents. It would be unfair to X to deprive
him of the experience of life with Mother during his formative years including
adolescence.

[
70
]

In closing, the Court does not agree with
counsel’s submission that Mother is angry because Father is standing in the way
when “she is ready to have X with her”. The Court can appreciate her
disappointment in Father’s actions. Mother left for Pakistan and relied on
Father’s word that X’s custody would be shared.

[
71
]

Mother's submission that Father's application
for custody was calculated may have merit. The Court does not condone the
manner in which Father instituted the proceedings. He sent the motion to Mother
while she was still in Pakistan on April 14, 2012. He wrote an email to Mother
on April 9, 2012, asking her to reconsider their agreement relating to X's
custody
[13]
. Contrary to Father's invitation, there was no time for further
discussion between the parties. The filing of Father Substitution of attorney
in January 30, 2014 leads the Court to believe that Father's proceedings were
planned and prepared prior to his email to Mother. However, Father's actions in
this regard are not relevant to the issue of X's best interest.

[
72
]

FOR THESE REASONS, THE COURT
:

[
73
]

GRANTS
in part,
Father’s motion for custody of X;

[
74
]

GRANT
S, in part,
Mother's motion to homologate the mediated agreement and to confirm joint
custody of X;

[
75
]

CONFIRMS
that the
parties shall continue to share joint custody of X;

[
76
]

DECLARES
that the
parties shall jointly exercise parental authority with respect to X and
ORDERS

them to consult a one another before making any important decisions relating to
the child, including but not limited to any decisions relating to his health
and or education;

[
77
]

ORDERS
that of
the residence of X shall alternate between the parties as follows:

a)

X shall maintain his primary residence with
the father during the school year, subject to the following residential time
with Mother:

b)

The summer school break each year with the
exception of the last week prior to the commencement of school;

c)

Thanksgiving weekend;

d)

American Thanksgiving weekend;

e)

One week at Christmas; it being understood
that the child shall be with Father for Christmas eve and Christmas day;

f)

Spring break;

g)

Easter;

h)

Memorial Day weekend;

i)

Any other time in the city
A, upon reasonable notice to Father.

[
78
]

ORDERS
that any
weekend contemplated above in b) to h) shall be extended in the event that the
weekend is preceded or followed by a pedagogical day;

[
79
]

ORDERS
the
parties to share equally the cost of plane flights for X related to the above
noted residential time with Mother;

[
80
]

AUTHORIZES
Mother
to communicate daily with X by way of video call or telephone. The timing of
such communication shall remain flexible in order to accommodate X's schedule
and activities;

[
81
]

ORDERS
that
custody of X be reviewed in 2018 prior to X's completion of primary school;

[
82
]

THE WHOLE
without
costs given the nature of the proceedings

KAREN KEAR
JODOIN, J.S.C.
